prompt_en: (ser/estar) He is boring (dull personality).
note: es aburrido = boring (a trait of the person); está aburrido = bored (how he feels right now)

prompt_en: (ser/estar) He is bored (right now).
note: está aburrido = feels bored now; es aburrido = is a boring person — same adjective, opposite meaning

prompt_en: (ser/estar) She is clever.
note: es lista = smart/clever; está lista = ready/prepared — a classic trap pair

prompt_en: (ser/estar) She is ready to go.
note: está lista = ready; es lista = clever — don't mix these up before a trip

prompt_en: (ser/estar) He is rich (wealthy).
note: es rico = wealthy (about a person); está rico = tastes delicious (about food) — same word, unrelated meanings

prompt_en: (ser/estar) The paella is delicious.
note: está rica = tastes great right now; es rica would drift toward 'is a wealthy paella', which is nonsense — food flavor always takes estar

prompt_en: (ser/estar) He is good-looking, in general.
note: es guapo = good-looking as a general trait; está guapo = looks good today (that haircut, that suit)

prompt_en: (ser/estar) He looks handsome today, in that suit.
note: está guapo = looks good today; es guapo = is good-looking in general — estar flags 'compared to usual'

prompt_en: (ser/estar) I am tired.
note: tired is always a state, never an identity — estar, not ser, no exceptions

prompt_en: (ser/estar) The party is at my house.
accept: la fiesta es en mi casa
reject: la fiesta está en mi casa
note: an event (party, meeting, concert) 'takes place' with ser + en; only physical objects/places use estar for location

prompt_en: (ser/estar) The bar is on Calle Mayor.
accept: el bar está en la calle mayor
reject: el bar es en la calle mayor
note: a physical place/object uses estar for location; contrast with events, which use ser + en (la fiesta es en...)

prompt_en: (ser/estar) Madrid is located in the center of Spain.
accept: Madrid está en el centro de España
reject: Madrid es en el centro de España
note: location of a real place is always estar, even for something as fixed as a capital city

prompt_en: (preterite) I went to Madrid last year.
accept: fui a Madrid el año pasado
reject: iba a Madrid el año pasado
note: fui = went (one completed trip, bounded by 'el año pasado'); iba = used to go / was going (habitual or background)

prompt_en: (imperfect) I used to go to Madrid every summer.
accept: iba a Madrid todos los veranos
note: a repeated, habitual action in the past ('every summer') calls for the imperfect, not the preterite

prompt_en: (preterite) I found out yesterday that she got married.
note: supe = found out (the moment the knowledge arrived); sabía = knew (an ongoing state of knowing)

prompt_en: (imperfect) I already knew that she was married.
note: sabía = knew, ongoing background knowledge; supe would mean 'found out', a wrong nuance here

prompt_en: (preterite) I met your brother at the party.
accept: conocí a tu hermano en la fiesta
reject: conocía a tu hermano en la fiesta
note: conocí = met (the first encounter, a completed event); conocía = knew/was acquainted with (ongoing)

prompt_en: (imperfect) I already knew your brother.
note: conocía = already was acquainted with; conocí would mean 'met for the first time', wrong here

prompt_en: (preterite) I tried to call you, but you didn't answer.
note: quise (preterite of querer) idiomatically means 'tried'; quería (imperfect) just means 'wanted', with no info about whether it happened

prompt_en: (imperfect) I wanted to go to the party, but I was tired.
accept: quería ir a la fiesta pero estaba cansado
quería ir a la fiesta pero estaba cansada
reject: quise ir a la fiesta pero estaba cansado
note: quería = wanted (ongoing desire, outcome unstated); quise would shift the meaning to 'tried and (usually) failed'

prompt_en: (preterite/imperfect) It was raining when I left the house.
note: the ongoing background condition (raining) is imperfect; the single completed action that interrupts it (left) is preterite

prompt_en: (preterite) The phone rang three times.
note: a specific, countable number of occurrences ('three times') is a bounded event — preterite, not imperfect

prompt_en: (imperfect) As a child, I played in the park every afternoon.
accept: de niño jugaba en el parque todas las tardes
de pequeño jugaba en el parque todas las tardes
reject: de niño jugué en el parque todas las tardes
note: a childhood habit repeated 'every afternoon' is classic imperfect territory, not a single completed event

prompt_en: (preterite) Yesterday I ate a huge paella.
note: 'ayer' anchors this to one completed, bounded event, so it takes the preterite even though eating can feel drawn-out

prompt_en: (subjunctive) I want you (tú) to call me tonight.
accept: quiero que me llames esta noche
reject: quiero que me llamas esta noche
note: quiero que + subjunctive whenever the subject of 'want' and the subject of the second verb are different people

prompt_en: (subjunctive) I hope you (vosotros) have a good trip.
accept: espero que tengáis un buen viaje
reject: espero que tenéis un buen viaje
note: esperar que always triggers the subjunctive — here the Peninsular vosotros subjunctive tengáis, not the indicative tenéis

prompt_en: (subjunctive) It's important that you (vosotros) arrive on time.
accept: es importante que lleguéis a tiempo
reject: es importante que llegáis a tiempo
note: impersonal expressions of importance/necessity (es importante que, es necesario que) trigger the subjunctive

prompt_en: (subjunctive) When I get home, I'll call you (tú) — hasn't happened yet.
accept: cuando llegue a casa te llamaré
reject: cuando llego a casa te llamaré
note: cuando + subjunctive for a future event that hasn't happened; cuando + indicative is for habitual or already-real events

prompt_en: (indicative) When I get home, I always call my mother — a daily habit.
accept: cuando llego a casa siempre llamo a mi madre
reject: cuando llegue a casa siempre llamo a mi madre
note: a habitual, already-established pattern uses cuando + indicative (llego); the subjunctive here would wrongly imply it hasn't happened yet

prompt_en: (subjunctive) I'm saving money so that we can travel in December.
accept: ahorro dinero para que podamos viajar en diciembre
voy a ahorrar dinero para que podamos viajar en diciembre
reject: ahorro dinero para que podemos viajar en diciembre
note: para que always triggers the subjunctive (podamos), never the indicative (podemos) — it introduces a purpose, not a fact

prompt_en: (subjunctive) I don't think he knows the answer.
accept: no creo que sepa la respuesta
reject: no creo que sabe la respuesta
note: no creo que + subjunctive (doubt/denial); compare creo que + indicative below when there's no doubt

prompt_en: (indicative) I think he knows the answer.
note: creo que (affirmative belief) takes the indicative; only the negated no creo que flips to subjunctive

prompt_en: (subjunctive) I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.
note: ojalá is always followed by the subjunctive, with or without que

prompt_en: (subjunctive) I hope you (tú) like the gift.
note: ojalá + subjunctive even with gustar-type verbs: te guste, not te gusta

prompt_en: (subjunctive) I need a flat that has an elevator (don't have one in mind yet).
accept: necesito un piso que tenga ascensor
reject: necesito un piso que tiene ascensor
note: subjunctive for an unspecified or hypothetical antecedent — a flat you haven't found yet

prompt_en: (indicative) I have a flat that has an elevator.
accept: tengo un piso que tiene ascensor
reject: tengo un piso que tenga ascensor
note: indicative for a specific, real antecedent you already have in mind — contrast with necesito un piso que tenga...

prompt_en: (subjunctive) It's possible that they arrive late.
note: es posible que expresses uncertainty and takes the subjunctive

prompt_en: (subjunctive) I want us to go to the beach this weekend.
accept: quiero que vayamos a la playa este fin de semana
reject: quiero que vamos a la playa este fin de semana
note: quiero que + subjunctive even with 'us' as the other subject: vayamos, not the indicative vamos

prompt_en: (por/para) I bought this for you (it's a gift for you).
note: para ti = intended recipient of the gift; por ti = on your behalf / because of you — different relationship

prompt_en: (por/para) I did it for you (on your behalf, because you couldn't).
note: por ti = in your place / because of you; para ti here would wrongly suggest the act itself was a gift

prompt_en: (por/para) We walked through the park.
note: por = motion through/along a space; para would mean heading toward the park as a destination

prompt_en: (por/para) I'm leaving for Madrid tomorrow.
note: para + destination; por here would mean 'through Madrid', not 'heading to Madrid'

prompt_en: (por/para) Thanks for the gift.
note: gracias por + [reason] is fixed — always por, never para

prompt_en: (por/para) This letter is for you.
note: para ti = intended recipient of the letter, exactly like the gift case above

prompt_en: (por/para) I paid twenty euros for the book.
accept: pagué veinte euros por el libro
reject: pagué veinte euros para el libro
note: por marks an exchange (money for a thing); para would sound like the money was made for the book

prompt_en: (por/para) In order to learn Spanish, you have to practice every day.
accept: para aprender español hay que practicar todos los días
reject: por aprender español hay que practicar todos los días
note: para + infinitive states a purpose/goal ('in order to'); por + infinitive would suggest a cause, which doesn't fit here

prompt_en: (por/para) I'll be there by Friday (deadline).
note: para + [deadline] = by that time; por + [day] would suggest 'sometime around Friday', a looser meaning

prompt_en: (por/para) He called by phone.
note: por = the means/medium used (phone, mail, email) — a fixed pattern, always por

prompt_en: (clitics) I want to give it to you (tú) — infinitive construction.
note: with a conjugated verb + infinitive, clitics either attach to the end of the infinitive or go before the conjugated verb — but they can never split the two, sitting between them

prompt_en: (clitics) I'm writing it to her right now — gerund construction.
note: same rule as infinitives: clitics attach to the gerund (with a written accent added) or precede the conjugated verb, never sit between the two verbs

prompt_en: (clitics) Give it to him! (tú command)
note: le + lo becomes se lo whenever both are third-person clitics — Spanish never allows 'le lo' back to back

prompt_en: (clitics) I already told it to them.
note: le/les + lo/la/los/las always becomes se lo/se la/etc. — 'le lo' is simply not a legal sequence in Spanish

prompt_en: (clitics) Can you (tú) pass it to me?
note: clitics go before the conjugated verb (me lo puedes) or attach to the infinitive (pasármelo) — never floating unattached in front of the infinitive

prompt_en: (clitics) I'm going to tell it to you (vosotros) tomorrow.
accept: os lo voy a decir mañana
reject: voy a os lo decir mañana
note: same infinitive rule with vosotros clitics: os lo before the conjugated verb, or attached as decíroslo — never split before the infinitive

prompt_en: (clitics) Tell it to me now! (tú command)
note: affirmative commands attach clitics to the end, in order indirect-then-direct (di + me + lo), with an accent added to keep the original stress

prompt_en: (clitics) Don't tell it to me!
note: negative commands never allow attached clitics — they always precede the verb, unlike affirmative commands

prompt_en: (gustar) I like the paella (singular thing liked).
note: gustar agrees with the THING liked, not with the person — one paella, so gusta

prompt_en: (gustar) I like the tapas (plural thing liked).
note: plural things liked need the plural verb: gustan, not gusta

prompt_en: (gustar) I love this bar.
note: encantar works exactly like gustar — it agrees with the singular thing loved, este bar, so encanta

prompt_en: (gustar) I'm missing two euros (I need two more euros).
note: faltar agrees with what's missing — dos euros is plural, so faltan

prompt_en: (gustar) I feel like going out tonight.
note: apetecer ('to feel like') is very Peninsular and works like gustar: me apetece + infinitive

prompt_en: (gustar) My head hurts.
note: doler agrees with the body part that hurts (la cabeza), not with the person — never conjugate it for 'yo'

prompt_en: (gustar) My feet hurt (plural).
note: plural body part needs the plural verb: duelen, not duele

prompt_en: (gustar) Do you (tú) like the beach?
note: gustar never conjugates to agree with the person (no 'gustas' here) — it always agrees with the thing liked, la playa

prompt_en: (hay) There are three cafés on this street.
accept: hay tres cafés en esta calle
hay tres cafeterías en esta calle
reject: tiene tres cafés en esta calle
note: hay = there is/are, for existence with no explicit subject; tener needs someone who possesses the thing

prompt_en: (tener) I have three brothers.
note: possession by a specific person uses tener; hay would strip out the 'I' entirely and just assert existence

prompt_en: (present perfect) I've already eaten today.
note: Peninsular Spanish uses the present perfect (he comido) for actions within a period that includes now, like 'today'; Latin America favors the simple preterite here

prompt_en: (hay) There's a problem with the reservation.
accept: hay un problema con la reserva
reject: tiene un problema con la reserva
note: an existing problem with no owner uses hay, not tiene

prompt_en: (hay) There's no milk left in the fridge.
accept: no hay leche en la nevera
reject: no tiene leche en la nevera
note: hay for what exists/doesn't exist in a place; tiene would need an explicit subject that possesses the milk

prompt_en: (tener) I am twenty-five years old.
note: age always uses tener + años in Spanish, never ser — a classic English-transfer error

prompt_en: (tener) I'm hungry.
note: hunger, like thirst and fear, is something you HAVE in Spanish (tengo hambre), not something you are

prompt_en: (tener) I'm cold.
note: tengo frío = I feel cold; estoy frío would literally describe your body as cold to the touch, a different (odd) meaning

prompt_en: (hace, weather) It's very hot today.
note: weather intensity is expressed with hacer (hace calor/frío/viento/sol), not ser or estar

prompt_en: (hace, time-ago) I arrived in Spain three days ago.
accept: llegué a España hace tres días
hace tres días llegué a España
reject: llegué a España desde tres días
note: 'ago' is hace + [time], usable before or after the clause; desde ('since') is a false-friend substitution that doesn't work here

prompt_en: (acabar de) I just ate (moments ago).
note: acabar de + infinitive = 'to have just done something', describing the immediate past

prompt_en: (soler) I usually go to the gym on Mondays.
accept: suelo ir al gimnasio los lunes
reject: solo ir al gimnasio los lunes
note: suelo (o→ue stem change of soler) = I usually [do]; solo = only/alone — easy to mix up in writing despite meaning nothing alike

prompt_en: (llevar + gerund) I've been living in Barcelona for three years.
accept: llevo tres años viviendo en Barcelona
reject: tengo tres años viviendo en Barcelona
note: llevar + [time] + gerund expresses an action that started in the past and still continues — a direct 'tengo X años' here is an English-transfer error

prompt_en: (llevar + gerund) How long have you (tú) been studying Spanish?
note: duration-so-far questions use llevar + gerund (llevas estudiando), not tener

prompt_en: (personal a) I'm looking for my keys.
note: personal a marks a direct object that is a specific person or pet — things never take it

prompt_en: (personal a + conocer) Do you (tú) know my sister?
note: for knowing people, use conocer (with personal a); saber is for facts and skills, not people
